1ed6550d6e:
This chapter is about promising something measurable for a system whose answers are not deterministic. It covers how to spend and protect the error budget behind that promise. It shows how to version and pin everything that changes behaviour: prompt, model, parameters, tools. It shows how to change any of them safely, with a gate, a canary and a rollback, and how to survive a provider's model deprecation.

Then it turns to the end of the lifecycle: documenting the system, handing it over, operating it and finally retiring it. Every decision is justified with a number from a requirements card. Telecom care and billing examples carry the chapter. Implementations are in Python and Java/Spring.
b15f41bf6d:
Reading time: 4 to 5 hours  ·  Companion code, 20 Python examples plus 2 Java ports for this chapter: ccarp-companion/16-documentation-slas-lifecycle/ (run bash run_all.sh; everything works offline).

The targets, prices, dates, notice periods and accuracies in the examples are illustrative planning numbers. Before any of them goes into a contract or an ADR, check the docs: the provider's model, pricing and deprecation pages. The exam facts for CCAR-P (item count, domain weights) come from third-party summaries of the published blueprint, so verify them against the official exam guide.
e688478a66:
The first sentence is the discipline.

A conventional service has one kind of failure that matters to the contract: it is down or slow. An AI service has a second, quieter kind. It is up and fast and wrong, in a way no health check sees. So the SLO set has to cover four families at once. The quality family has to be measured by sampling, which means its numbers carry sampling error, and the alerting must respect that.

The second sentence is the pressure. Models are retired. Behaviour shifts between snapshots. Prices change. The only defence is to be able to answer three questions at any moment, and in minutes: what exactly is running, what do we know about how well it works, and how do we get back to the previous state?
a0470f5ec0:
The blueprint for Domain 6 asks the architect to do five things:

  • lead structured discovery and requirements;
  • communicate decisions and trade-offs;
  • set up feedback loops and manage expectations, including SLAs;
  • produce documentation and implementation guidance;
  • manage the lifecycle from discovery through design, handoff, monitoring and iteration.

Chapter 1 covered discovery and the requirements card. This chapter covers the back half of the lifecycle: what you promise, how you keep the promise, how you change the system without breaking it, and how you hand it over and retire it.

Where a topic has its own chapter, this one shows where it plugs in and points there for the mechanics. Observability and usage metadata are in ch 10. Evaluation sets and statistics are in ch 11. A/B tests, shadow traffic and cost-latency optimisation are in ch 12. Guardrails, kill switches and human review are in ch 13. Retention, documentation duties and audit are in ch 14.
39b4ac0bd5:
A Spring architect will recognise the shape. An SLI is a Micrometer meter. An SLO is a threshold on a timer or a counter ratio. The error budget is the part of the contract that engineering may spend on risk. The policy is the change-advisory rule that everyone agreed to before the incident, rather than argued about during it.

Only one thing is new. Two of the four meters cannot be read off the request path: quality, and to a lesser extent cost. Quality needs a judge or a human. Cost needs usage metadata joined to a business outcome.
572923564b:
The reader's own industry wrote the first chapter. Circuit switches were built to a reliability target that sounded absurd to computing people. The often-quoted design goal for electronic switching systems of the 1960s and 1970s was about two hours of downtime in forty years. 'Five nines', 99.999 percent availability, is about 5.3 minutes a year, and it became the shorthand for carrier grade.

The number is not the lesson that carried over. The lesson is that availability was defined per call, measured at the edge, and tied to a procedure for what to do when it slipped.

Service level agreements as contracts followed in the 1980s and 1990s, as outsourcing and managed services spread. The ITIL practice framework started as a UK government effort in the late 1980s. It gave IT organisations the vocabulary that this chapter reuses: service levels, change management, release management and configuration management.
5bffb644a9:
Google's Site Reliability Engineering book (2016) and its follow-up workbook (2018) made two moves that matter here.

First, they separated three things: the indicator (what you measure), the objective (the internal target) and the agreement (the contract with consequences). And they insisted that the objective be stricter than the agreement.

Second, they turned the leftover (one minus the objective) into an error budget that the product team may spend on change. That converts the old argument between 'ship' and 'be stable' into arithmetic.

Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerting came from the workbook: a fast burn pages, a slow burn opens a ticket. It is the alerting design used in section 09. Check the workbook before copying its exact thresholds.
d4ff95b59f:
In parallel, the machine-learning community had learned that models fail in ways their authors do not announce. 'Datasheets for Datasets' (Gebru and colleagues, 2018) and 'Model Cards for Model Reporting' (Mitchell and colleagues, 2019) proposed short standard documents. Each states intended use, evaluation by subgroup, and known limitations.

The per-subgroup evaluation table is the idea that survives in this chapter. An aggregate number is a summary, and it can hide the segment where harm happens.

Regulation later turned documentation into a duty for some systems. The example to know is the EU AI Act's technical documentation requirements for high-risk systems. Ask counsel, and see ch 14, for which obligations apply to your system.
f6bd5595a5:
Model registries appeared around 2019 to 2020 to answer one question: which model version is in production, and where did it come from? MLflow's registry is the widely used example.

Then prompts became the main behaviour-defining artefact of LLM applications, and teams rediscovered every lesson of configuration management. Prompts were edited in place in a database. Prompt text lived in a YAML file nobody reviewed. A model name silently pointed at a newer snapshot.

By 2024 and 2025 the practice had converged. A prompt, its model, its parameters and its tool schemas are treated as a single versioned release bundle, with an evaluation report attached. That is the design in section 11.
ff6fae7616:
Hosted models add a constraint that a library dependency does not have. The provider can announce that a model version will stop being served on a given date, and then it does. Providers publish deprecation pages and notice periods. The current policy and dates for Anthropic models are on its model deprecations page; check the docs.

So every system built on a hosted model needs a standing migration capability, not a one-off project. And every SLA that depends on the model needs a clause that acknowledges it. That is the difference between a documentation chapter and a lifecycle chapter.
ec90c58575:
Start from the failure the contract is meant to cover. A payment API fails by returning errors or by being slow. Both are visible in the request path. Both are binary per request. A rate over a window is a complete description of health.

A language-model service adds a third state that is neither success nor error. It is a well-formed, fast, confident answer that is wrong, unsafe, out of policy, or simply worse than last week. The HTTP status is 200 and every dependency is green. If the SLO set contains only availability and latency, the service can break what the customer cares about for days while every dashboard stays green.
91c4dd9bd9:
Three further properties change how the objectives are written.

Outputs are not deterministic. Even with temperature at zero, providers do not generally guarantee bit-identical outputs across runs (check the docs for your model). So a single test result is a sample, not a fact. Quality must be a rate over many items with a confidence interval, and any gate must measure run-to-run noise (ch 11).

Behaviour changes without a deploy. The model can change under a floating alias. A retrieval index can be rebuilt. A tool can return different data. The prompt can be edited in a console. Each of these changes production behaviour, and the conventional deploy pipeline never sees any of them.

Cost is a function of behaviour. Suppose a prompt edit moves a volatile value to the top of the system prompt. That breaks the cache prefix and doubles the bill, with no change in correctness (ch 5). So cost is not a finance report. It is an operational signal with its own SLO.
c456309cbc:
The exam angle has two common shapes. A scenario may describe a system whose dashboards are green while customers complain. The missing element is almost always a quality SLI, measured on sampled production traffic by segment. More infrastructure monitoring is not the answer.

Or a scenario may describe a contract that promises '98 percent accuracy'. The answer is almost always to replace the guarantee with a measured SLO, a reporting method and a remediation process (section 10).
ceb8094369:
A service level indicator is a ratio of good events to eligible events. Both words in that sentence are decisions.

Eligible says which requests count: all of them, or only chat, or everything except requests the customer cancelled. Good says what a good event is. It has to be precise enough that two engineers computing it from the same logs get the same number. Most disputes about SLOs are really disputes about one of these two definitions. That is why the specification below forces both to be written down.

An objective is then a target for that ratio over a window. A good objective also names its owner and what happens when it is missed.
8e07a045d9:
Take the four families in turn.

Availability: a request is good if it produced a valid response. That means HTTP success, a schema-valid body, within a hard timeout of 30 seconds, and not served by a fallback that the contract excludes. Define 'valid' at the edge, after your own validators. That is the difference between measuring the model's uptime and measuring the customer's experience. A 200 with an unparseable body is a bad event.

Latency: never an average. Say 'share of chat requests answered within 6 seconds (time to last token)'. The percentile is then implicit, and the arithmetic is a plain ratio, which a histogram metric can also compute exactly. If streaming is used, distinguish time to first token (what the user feels) from time to last token (what a downstream system waits for). Set separate objectives for each.

Quality: the share of sampled responses passing a rubric, per segment. The sampling plan is part of the definition.

Cost: spend per business outcome (resolved conversation, processed invoice), not spend per request. A change that halves cost per request and doubles retries has not saved anything.
5c3d8427ab:
Per-segment floors are the part CCAR-P exams like to test, because they are literal. Say the requirements card says 'dispute handling must be at least 92 percent'. An aggregate quality SLO of 94 percent does not satisfy it. A service at 96 percent in four segments and 88 percent in the dispute segment passes the aggregate and breaks the requirement.

So the specification carries floors per segment, and the linter rejects a quality SLO without them.
95c32fb710:
The linter is deliberately boring. Its value is that the review comment 'your latency SLI is an average' stops being an opinion. It becomes a failing check in the pull request that changes the spec.

Treat the spec as code. It lives in the repository next to the alert rules that implement it. Changes to it go through review by the owners of the affected SLOs. And the generated documentation (section 17) is built from it, so the contract and the monitoring cannot drift apart.
2c499b0706:
Quality cannot be read from the request path, so it is measured on a sample. Some fraction of production responses is scored by an automated judge, a rubric check, or a human. The SLI is the pass proportion in the sample.

Now the sample size, not the model, decides what you can know. A proportion estimated from n items has a standard error of about sqrt(p(1-p)/n). Take 400 judged responses a day and a true pass rate of 94 percent. The standard error is about 1.2 percentage points, and a 95 percent interval is about plus or minus 2.3 points. A day that comes in at 92 percent is eight responses worse than expected. That is entirely consistent with an unchanged system.
d4e5327a79:
Two consequences follow. Both show up on the exam, as 'the alert is too noisy' or 'the alert never fires'.

First, the alert must not compare a point estimate to the target. Suppose the system sits exactly at 94 percent and you compare each daily pass rate to 94 percent. You page on roughly half of all days, because the estimate is below the target half the time. In the simulation below that is about thirteen false pages a month.

Second, the window must contain enough samples to see the burn rate you care about. A burn rate of 6 against a 6 percent allowance means 36 percent of responses are failing. That is easy to see in a hundred samples. A burn rate of 2 still exhausts the monthly budget in fifteen days, and it means 12 percent failing. A window of a hundred samples cannot reliably tell 12 percent from 6 percent.

The function min_detectable_burn computes the smallest burn rate a window of n samples can separate from 'within budget' at three standard errors.
670b146908:
The remedy for a thin sample is rarely 'judge more'. Judging costs money: an LLM judge call per response, plus calibration against human labels (see ch 11). So choose the sample size from the smallest burn rate you want to catch, in the time you can tolerate.

With 400 samples a day, a burn of about 1.8 is visible at the end of one day, and a burn of 1.45 at the end of three. That matches the slow-burn ticket policy in section 09. To catch a burn of 2 within six hours, you need about 100 samples every six hours, which is 400 a day. The arithmetic and the policy agree.

If the requirement is tighter, stratify the sample. Over-sample the high-risk segments and weight them back for the aggregate. And keep a smaller always-on check for the segment with the hardest floor.
0f425842ad:
Two further cautions.

A judge model is itself a measuring instrument, with its own bias and drift. Calibrate it against a human-labelled set on a schedule. Treat a change of judge model as a change to the SLI definition, which resets the baseline (ch 11).

And if the team can improve a quality SLI by editing the judge prompt, that SLI will be improved that way. Keep the rubric and the judge under the same change control as the system under test.
27d2b87ef3:
The average latency of an LLM service describes almost no request. The reason is structural. Response time is the sum of three parts:

  • a prompt-processing time that grows with input length;
  • a generation time that grows with output length;
  • for agentic or tool-using flows, a number of extra round trips that depends on what the model decides to do.

The result is a mixture. In the simulation below, 85 percent of requests are plain answers near 1.8 seconds, and 15 percent use a tool near 5.5 seconds. The mean is 2.5 seconds, a value almost nobody experiences. The p95 is 6.4 seconds, which is the experience of the tool-using slice. A latency SLO written on the mean would pass while one customer in seven waits more than five seconds.
8ddee52d12:
The second structural fact is about aggregation: percentiles cannot be averaged. Say instance A (mostly plain answers) has a p95 of 4.1 seconds and instance B (mostly tool calls) has 8.9. The fleet p95 is not 6.5. It is 5.6, because it depends on how many requests each instance served.

The only form of latency data that merges correctly across instances, time and pods is a histogram with fixed bucket boundaries. That is why the SLI is written as 'share of requests within 6 seconds'. It is a ratio of two counters, one of them a bucket of the histogram, and it can be summed across anything.

The cost is resolution. A quantile estimated from buckets is only as precise as the bucket width. So place a bucket boundary exactly at each objective threshold.
e892f81488:
Set latency objectives per request class, not globally. A chat answer, a tool-using investigation and a batch summarisation each have different humans (or machines) waiting on them. For machine consumers, apply the thresholds to time to last token. When a person watches the text appear, apply them to both time to first token and time to last token.

When an objective is missed, the diagnosis follows the structure above. Look at four things:

  • input tokens (retrieval size, history);
  • output tokens (verbosity changes after a prompt or model change);
  • the number of model round trips (an agent that started taking one more step);
  • provider-side latency.

Ch 10 shows the traces that separate them, and ch 12 covers the optimisations.
e4fd7b425d:
Cost belongs in the SLO set for the same reason the other three do. It can degrade silently, and eventually it hurts the customer, either through price or through the budget owner cancelling the project.

The SLI is spend per business outcome. Spend per request is too easy to game and too hard to compare across changes. The denominator in the example is a resolved conversation. That also keeps the metric honest when a change improves cost per request but lowers the resolution rate.
2923e76a12:
The simulation below shows why you want this SLO at all. On day five a prompt edit puts a volatile value near the top of the system prompt. The cached prefix no longer matches. The cache hit rate falls from 72 percent to 3 percent, and cost per resolved conversation goes from $0.028 to $0.052. Quality is unchanged, latency rises slightly, and no functional test fails.

The cost SLO says a day is good if spend per resolved conversation is at most $0.032, and 95 percent of days must be good. Under that SLO, three bad days exhaust a budget of 1.5 days.

The diagnosis is in the usage metadata: the field that reports tokens read from the cache collapsed. For field names, check the docs for the current usage object, and see ch 5 for cache design.
01500f0ea3:
Two design rules follow.

Alert on the leading indicators (cache hit rate, average input tokens per call, calls per conversation) as well as on the lagging one (dollars per resolved conversation). The leading ones identify the cause, and they arrive within minutes.

And make the cost SLO's policy a review, not a freeze. Unlike quality or availability, a cost breach is rarely an emergency. Treating it like one trains the team to ignore the policy. The example spec uses 'review-on-breach' for exactly that reason.
de63cbe8bd:
An SLO of 99.5 percent says that 0.5 percent of events may be bad. Over a 30-day window with 1.2 million requests, that is 6,000 bad requests. Expressed as time at full outage, it is 3.6 hours. This leftover is the error budget.

Its purpose is behavioural. Without it, reliability and velocity are argued about in the abstract. With it, the team can say 'we have spent 70 percent of the budget on a provider incident, so the model swap waits'. Or: 'we have spent 4 percent in three weeks, so we can ship the risky change this week'.

The budget makes the trade-off visible, and it cuts both ways. An SLO that is never missed is a sign that the target is too loose or the team is too cautious.
9d935c8440:
The budget is also the unit for comparing incidents. The simulation shows a provider incident in which 60 percent of requests fail for 55 minutes at three times average traffic. It consumes 2,750 bad requests in under an hour. That is 46 percent of the monthly availability budget. Add a retry-and-fallback path that rescues 70 percent of the failed requests, and the same incident consumes 825, or 14 percent.

That is the argument for resilience engineering, expressed in the currency the business uses. It is also how to justify the cost of a second model route in an ADR. Take the expected number of such incidents per year and multiply it by the budget the route saves. If that is worth more than the route's standing cost, the second route pays for itself (ch 6 and ch 13 cover the fallback designs).
35e7b5146c:
The policy has four rungs, agreed in advance with product and operations:

  • more than half the budget left: ship normally;
  • 10 to 50 percent left: no risky change (model swap, prompt rewrite, new tool) without approval from the service owner;
  • under 10 percent: only reliability work and rollbacks;
  • exhausted: freeze, write a postmortem, and fund a reliability item before new features.

Two details make the policy usable. The budget is per SLO family, so an exhausted cost budget does not freeze reliability work. And the budget is read before a change is scheduled, not after. The change-management section (13) makes 'budget remaining' an input to the gate.
9ec70be0bc:
The burn rate is the observed bad fraction divided by the allowed bad fraction. A burn of 1 exhausts the budget exactly at the end of the window. A burn of 14.4 sustained for an hour consumes 14.4 / 720 = 2 percent of a 30-day budget.

The workbook pattern pairs a long window with a short one, and fires only when both exceed the threshold. The long window establishes that the burn is large enough to matter. The short window establishes that it is still happening, so the alert clears within minutes of the fix instead of an hour later.

The three standard rows are:

  • 1 hour / 5 minutes at 14.4 (page);
  • 6 hours / 30 minutes at 6 (page);
  • 3 days / 6 hours at 1 (ticket).

They correspond to spending 2, 5 and 10 percent of the budget. Check the workbook for the rationale before copying the numbers; the structure is what matters.
9426ef53c3:
Compare a naive alert: 'error rate over 5 minutes above 1 percent'. The simulation exposes three weaknesses.

It pages on a 5-minute blip that costs a tenth of a percent of the budget. In a clean two-day stretch with 0.2 percent background errors, it fires 19 times. The burn-rate policy fires zero times.

It pays no attention to size. Take a 40-hour slow burn at 1.2 percent, which costs 13 percent of the budget. The naive alert pages at minute 15 and then keeps paging. The policy opens a ticket after 16 hours, which is the right urgency.

And it cannot tell an incident that will exhaust the budget in two days from one that will not exhaust it in two months.
c4b375640a:
Apply the sample-size lesson from section 05 to the quality row. A quality burn-rate alert needs a minimum number of samples in each window before it is allowed to fire. The library's evaluate takes min_n and reports 'insufficient-data' otherwise. At 400 samples a day, the fast row (1 hour) simply does not exist for a sampled SLI.

Instead, use 6 hours / 1 hour at a burn of 6 as the fast page, and 3 days / 12 hours at a burn of 1.5 as the ticket. Section 19 estimates the page rate this produces.
4d284875cb:
The SLA is the SLO with a customer attached. Three rules govern it.

It is looser than the SLO. The internal objective then breaches first, which gives the team time to act before money moves. In the example the internal availability objective is 99.5 percent (3.6 hours of budget a month) and the contractual commitment is 99.0 percent (7.2 hours). That leaves 3.6 hours of headroom.

It is measured where the customer experiences the service: at your edge, after your own validation, with a precise definition of exclusions. Exclusions cover scheduled maintenance and customer-caused errors. Provider events count as exclusions only to the extent your provider agreement actually covers you. Check that agreement. A carrier-grade promise built on a provider's best-effort terms is a liability.

And it has a remedy ladder: service credits by tier. That makes the cost of a breach a number the business can price.
9f5e4bf801:
The AI-specific question is what to commit to for the parts that depend on model behaviour.

Availability and latency can be committed to in the usual way. Write the latency commitment as a percentile on a defined request class: for example, 95 percent of chat requests answered within 8 seconds at the edge, excluding long-context batch jobs.

Accuracy is different. A contractual guarantee of '98 percent accuracy' invites three problems. The metric is not defined: accuracy on what distribution, judged by whom? The measurement is noisy (section 05). And the model can change on the provider's schedule.

The defensible commitment is to a method and a process. That means the measurement method and sample, the reporting cadence, and a per-segment floor. Below the floor, the vendor team must open a remediation plan within a stated time. Add a notice period for changes that alter behaviour. Quality stays an internal SLO. Externally, it becomes an SLI report plus a remediation clause.
212d010304:
R is responsible, A is accountable (one per row), C is consulted, I is informed.

The row to notice is deprecation tracking. It needs one accountable owner. 'Everyone saw the email' is the usual cause of a migration that starts with three weeks left. Route the provider's deprecation feed into a ticketing queue owned by the platform team, not into an inbox.
766c52877c:
After any complaint, the first operational question is 'what was the system when this happened?' For a conventional service the answer is a commit hash and a container tag.

For an AI service the commit hash is not enough. Behaviour is defined by at least five things, and they change on different cadences:

  • the prompt text;
  • the model snapshot;
  • the sampling and length parameters;
  • the tool schemas and permissions;
  • the data the prompt is built from (retrieval index, few-shot store, policy tables).

A change in any of them can change quality, latency and cost. Several of them do not live in the application repository at all.
8f049b71f0:
The design that works is the release bundle. It is a single immutable record that names the prompt by content hash, the model by pinned snapshot, the parameters, the hash of the tool schemas, the owner, and the evaluation report that admitted it.

Everything downstream refers to the bundle id: the canary, the dashboards, the logs, the system card, the rollback. A request log line that carries bundle=billing-explainer@2 answers the first question in one query. A log line that carries only a model name does not.
935a855d96:
Three rules make the registry trustworthy.

Pin snapshots, never aliases. A moving alias is a deploy you did not make, so the registry refuses it. Which ids are stable snapshots and which are aliases is a fact from the provider's model pages. The registry reads it from a catalog the team fills from the docs (check the docs). Do not hard-code the assumption that a name with a date in it is stable, or that one without a date is not.

Hash the content. The bundle stores the hash of the prompt text, and the service verifies the hash at start-up. An edit in place, in a console or a database row, then fails the check instead of silently becoming production.

One active bundle per prompt id. Promoting a new one demotes the old one to 'deprecated'. That is also exactly the state a rollback needs to return to.
c3763b34fd:
For operations, a monotonic integer per prompt id is enough: billing-explainer@1, @2, @3. The content hash is the real identity.

Semantic versioning (major.minor.patch) is tempting. But it needs a definition of 'breaking' that matches a prompt's contract. If you want it, define it by the output contract and the evaluation delta:

  • a major version changes the output schema or the tool set, so downstream code must change;
  • a minor version changes behaviour inside the same contract and passes the gate;
  • a patch changes only wording that the gate shows is neutral.

Do not invent compatibility promises you cannot test. The simplest rule that survives audits: the integer increases on every promotion, the hash proves the content, and the change class (section 13) is recorded with it.
4761b2b178:
A registry is only as good as the code that uses it. The second control is a linter that scans the code base for the ways pinning gets bypassed:

  • a floating alias;
  • a model id hard-coded next to the call site;
  • an inline prompt literal;
  • prompt text in configuration;
  • a reference to a model with an announced retirement date.

Run it in CI and on a schedule. The schedule matters, because a retirement notice arrives after the code was merged.
c095475aa8:
Lifecycle management starts from a small state machine. Most failures are an illegal transition. A candidate that was never evaluated goes to production. A deprecated bundle is deleted while it is still the rollback target. A retired model is still referenced by a nightly job.

Five states cover it. Candidate: registered, not serving users. Canary: serving a small, controlled share of traffic, admitted by a gate report. Active: the one bundle serving the default route, admitted by a canary report. Deprecated: superseded but still servable. This is the rollback target, and it waits out its rollback window here. Retired: not serving, references removed, archive complete.
c075fe8688:
Each transition has a precondition expressed as evidence, not as a person's say-so:

  • candidate to canary needs an upgrade-gate report id;
  • canary to active needs a canary report id;
  • active to deprecated happens automatically when a successor becomes active;
  • deprecated to active is a rollback, and needs only a reason;
  • deprecated to retired needs the retirement checklist of section 20.

The registry in the previous section enforces the first three in code. Process and the retirement check enforce the rest.
eb300a24da:
Change management for an AI service answers two questions before the change happens. What could this change affect? And what evidence do we need before it reaches users?

The answers vary a lot. A typo in a runbook cannot alter a model answer. A rewording of the system prompt can alter every answer. A model snapshot swap can alter every answer, every latency, every token count and every refusal. A new tool changes what the system is able to do, so it is a security question as well as a quality question. A change to a guardrail policy changes the safety envelope.

Treat all five alike, and you either slow down the trivial change or under-review the dangerous one.
a7634cffd7:
So classify by what the change can alter, and attach gates and approvers to the class. The classification in the companion code is deliberately mechanical. It looks at which artefacts changed and takes the highest class:

  • C0 is documentation only.
  • C1 is prompt wording, few-shot examples, retrieval configuration or output schema. It needs the golden set, a per-segment check and owner approval.
  • C2 is model or sampling parameters. It needs everything in C1, plus latency, cost, behaviour diff and shadow replay, with AI-quality approval.
  • C3 is tool schema, scope or permissions. It needs C1 plus a security review and a red-team run (ch 13), with security approval.
  • C4 is guardrail or policy. It needs C1 plus red-team and compliance review, with compliance approval (ch 14).
62d0095f26:
The rule in the last two lines of the example saves the most time in practice. Suppose a pull request swaps the model and rewrites the prompt, and the gate then shows a regression in one segment. Nobody can say which change caused it.

So split the change. First move the model with the prompt unchanged, to see what the model does to the old prompt. Then edit the prompt on the new model. This costs one extra gate run and removes the argument.

The exception is a prompt change that the new model forces: a parameter it no longer accepts, or an output format it has to be told about. In that case the forced edit goes in first, alone, on the old model, and is gated as C1.
a731d55124:
A rollback that works at 03:00 has four properties.

It is a pointer flip in the registry, not a build and deploy. The previous bundle is already packaged and its hash verified.

It is fast: seconds to flip, plus the cache warm-up time of the previous prompt prefix. Your cost SLO will show a transient.

It is possible. The previous bundle's model snapshot must still be served by the provider. That is why the cutover must complete, and the rollback window elapse, before the old model's retirement date (section 16).

And it is rehearsed. The runbook's rollback step is executed in a staging environment on a schedule, and the date of the last rehearsal is in the runbook front matter (section 18). A rollback that has never been executed is a hope.
8c6d4d4dc0:
Be explicit about what a rollback does not undo. Responses already sent stay sent. Cases already created by an agent's tool calls stay created. Embeddings or indices rebuilt for the new prompt remain.

If the change had side effects, the runbook needs the compensating action (ch 13 on tool gates and reversibility). The change record should list those side effects before approval.
716fcbec0c:
The gate is where the lifecycle meets statistics. It answers one question. Given results from the candidate bundle and the active bundle on the same golden set, is the candidate acceptable in every segment, on every metric, with enough evidence to say so?

The word every is the design. An aggregate score can improve while the segment that carries the contractual risk regresses. And the aggregate is weighted by the golden set's mix, which is deliberately not the traffic mix: high-risk segments are over-sampled so that they have a chance of being measured at all.

So the gate evaluates per segment. It reweights to traffic only for the aggregate line. And it treats a missing sample size as a result (inconclusive), not as a pass.
e25c71bcf3:
The statistical test is paired, because both bundles run on the same items. For each segment, count the items the baseline passes and the candidate fails (b), and the reverse (c). The estimated difference is (c - b) / n.

Its standard error comes from the discordant counts. Only items on which the two bundles disagree carry information about the difference. That is why a paired test needs far fewer items than comparing two independent proportions.

A one-sided 95 percent lower bound on the difference is compared to the negative margin. If the lower bound is above minus the margin, the candidate is non-inferior in that segment. The architect can defend that statement: 'with 95 percent confidence the candidate is no more than 2 points worse in dispute handling'.

The harness checks four more things. The candidate's own Wilson lower bound must clear the segment's absolute floor. The candidate's p95 must clear the segment's latency objective. The cost per request ratio must stay under a ceiling. And the run-to-run flake rate must stay low enough for the scores to mean something.
1f263e25b9:
Read the first table the way a reviewer would. The candidate improves four segments, and it lifts the traffic-weighted aggregate by 1.3 points (0.9412 to 0.9546). On that line alone it would be approved.

In the dispute segment, though, it is 2.5 points worse. The lower bound of the difference is minus 4.8 points against a margin of 2, and the verdict is REJECT. The aggregate hid the regression because dispute handling is 10 percent of traffic.

After the simulated prompt fix, the dispute segment's difference is +1.1 points, with a lower bound of minus 1.2. That is inside the margin. But the verdict is HOLD, not ADMIT, because 360 items cannot certify a 2-point margin. That is the correct behaviour, and it is why the harness has a min_n per segment.
e3ea6838bb:
For a paired non-inferiority test with a true difference of zero, the sample size is approximately n = (zalpha + zbeta)2 q / delta2. Here q is the discordant rate (the share of items on which exactly one bundle passes), and delta is the margin. The z values are 1.645 for a one-sided 5 percent test and 0.84 for 80 percent power.

With q = 0.08, a margin of 5 points needs about 200 items. A margin of 2 points needs about 1,240. A margin of 1 point needs almost 5,000. The sample size scales with the inverse square of the margin, so halving the margin quadruples the labelling bill.

That is the number that connects a business requirement ('dispute handling must not get worse') to a budget line (labelled items).
3a76b42342:
So the architect faces a trade-off with a price tag. For the four standard segments, the existing golden set can certify a 5-point margin. For the high-risk segment there are two choices. Accept a wider margin, and document why the requirement allows it. Or invest roughly 880 labelled items, about $3,300 in the example, once, to certify a 2-point margin on every future upgrade.

The golden set is reused for each prompt edit, model upgrade and vendor change, so the cost amortises quickly. A quarterly upgrade cadence pays it back in the first year. Put that justification in the ADR, with the numbers, rather than 'we need a bigger test set'. (Ch 11 covers building and maintaining golden sets, including leakage and drift.)
0e65f554a8:
The gate works on a fixed golden set. The canary works on live traffic. They find different problems.

The gate finds the regressions the team thought to test for. The canary finds the ones it did not: an input pattern absent from the golden set, a load-dependent latency effect, an interaction with a real tool backend, a refusal pattern triggered by real customer language.

So the canary is not a smaller gate. It is a different instrument. Its design question is how long it must run, and how much traffic it needs, to be informative.
0ec619718a:
Derive stage length from sample counts. A stage cannot pass its quality check until it has accumulated a minimum number of judged samples (300 in the example). It should also run at least one full daily cycle (24 hours), so that diurnal traffic differences are included.

Judged samples arrive at a rate of requests per hour, times the traffic share, times the judge rate. When the traffic share is tiny, judge every request. When it is large, sample.

The stage table judges at 100, 50, 10 and 1 percent for the 1, 5, 25 and 100 percent stages. With those rates, every stage is bounded by the 24-hour minimum rather than by sample accumulation, and the total minimum rollout is four days. Judging only 2 percent at the 1 percent stage would have required 900 hours.
7400eb1a9d:
Be precise about what the canary can detect. At 300 to 400 samples the Wilson interval is plus or minus 2.5 to 3 points. So the canary guards against gross regression. A candidate truly at 90 percent, against a baseline of 94, is rolled back within the first stage, after about 400 exposed requests (0.03 percent of a month). But the canary cannot see a 2-point drop.

Subtle regressions are the gate's job. That is why the gate and the canary use different thresholds, and why neither replaces the other.

The canary's advance rule is a lower bound above a floor. Its rollback rule is an upper bound below the baseline. Anything in between holds the stage. It never advances by default.
f9e383a6e0:
A deprecation notice starts a clock that you do not control. The mistake is to treat it as a project to schedule when someone has time. The correct treatment is to compute the critical path backwards from the retirement date, and to check the slack on the day the notice arrives.

The example uses a model announced on 8 October, with retirement after 15 December: 68 days. (The real notice period and dates for any model are on the provider's deprecations page, so check the docs. The number here is a planning figure.) Working backwards:

  • a 7-day rollback window after cutover, while the old model is still served;
  • a 7-day canary and cutover;
  • 14 days of shadow replay and gate;
  • 14 days of prompt adaptation and re-evaluation;
  • 14 days to top up the golden set for the high-risk segment;
  • 5 days of candidate selection and inventory.

The critical path is 61 days against 68 on the calendar. That is a slack of 7 days, 10 percent.
1eddca8374:
The slack rule in the example is that slack must be at least 25 percent of the calendar. Review cycles, incidents and holidays consume the first 20 percent, whatever the plan says. By that rule the verdict is START NOW.

The per-dependent view makes it concrete. The dispute assistant has a 38-day path of its own, so its latest start is 31 October, 23 days away.

This is the argument for a standing capability. Have a golden set that is already large enough, a replay harness that already exists, and bundles that already have owners. Those turn a 61-day path into a 25-day one. The quarterly upgrade rehearsal keeps the capability warm: run the gate against the newest candidate model, whether or not a deprecation has been announced.
b5066b1738:
A model upgrade is a vendor change. The change plan is the same whether the trigger is a deprecation, a price change, or a new model the team wants:

  • Phase 1, inventory: list every bundle, job and notebook that references the model (the pin linter), with its owner and its risk tier.
  • Phase 2, selection: choose the candidate by running the segment-level cost-quality comparison from ch 4, not by name.
  • Phase 3, offline regression: run the golden set on the candidate with the old prompt, unchanged. Then run the paired test.
  • Phase 4, behaviour diff on replayed production traffic: this catches what scores do not.
  • Phase 5, adaptation: edit the prompt for the new model as a separate C1 change.
  • Phase 6, shadow and canary.
  • Phase 7, cutover and rollback window.
  • Phase 8, retire the old pin.
8a30b62839:
Phase 4 deserves its own example, because it is where silent regressions hide. Replay sampled production prompts through both models and compare behaviour, not quality. That finds things the golden set does not measure.

In the example the quality score is not computed at all. The diff shows four things about the new model:

  • it sometimes wraps its JSON in a code fence, so a strict parser rejects 11.7 percent of responses;
  • it refuses 1.7 percent of prompts;
  • it calls a tool on 11.7 percent of prompts that the old model answered directly;
  • it writes about twice as many output tokens, so the cost and latency models are wrong.

Each is a fix in the harness or the prompt, not a model problem. The fixes are tolerant parsing or structured outputs (check the docs for the current feature), a refusal route, a tool-call review, and a recomputed cost estimate.
9e0bc86240:
Documentation fails in two predictable ways. Either it is written once and drifts, so the architecture diagram shows a model that was retired in March. Or it is a pile of everything, so the one fact the on-call engineer needs at 03:00 is on page 40 of a document named 'final-v3'.

The cure for both is to decide three things for each document. Who reads it, and when? Who owns it? Can it be generated from a source of truth?

Anything that can be generated from the registry, the SLO spec, the evaluation reports or the alert catalog should be. A generated document cannot disagree with the system. What remains for humans is the reasoning: why this pattern, why this margin, what we decided not to do.
8d78434e9f:
A model card describes a model. But what your customer relies on is a system: a model, a prompt, tools, retrieval, guardrails and humans. So the card to write is a system card for the assistant. It states:

  • the intended use and the explicit exclusions;
  • the versions (model snapshot, prompt hash, bundle hash);
  • the evaluation by segment, with intervals, the date and the golden-set version;
  • the known limitations, in plain language;
  • the human-oversight arrangements;
  • the data handled and its retention;
  • the change history;
  • the contacts.

The evaluation table is the part inherited from the model-card literature. It is also the part most often cut for space. Keep it: per-segment results with intervals are what a sceptical reader checks first.
bd88b1cedf:
Two notes on honesty.

A card that says nothing about limitations is a marketing page, and a regulator or a customer's risk team will read it that way. Write at least the failure modes you have actually observed, such as the weaker proration segment in the example.

And the card is a snapshot. Generate it at release, store it with the bundle, and never edit it afterwards. When the numbers change, there is a new bundle and a new card.

A legal duty to maintain technical documentation may apply, for example under the EU AI Act for high-risk systems. If so, the card is an input to that file, not a substitute for it. Ask counsel and see ch 14.
7877a77667:
A runbook is read under stress by someone who may not know the system. That fact dictates the form.

  • The title is the alert name, so the page leads to the runbook without search.
  • The first section states the symptom in terms of the alert, then the customer impact. The impact tells the responder how fast to move.
  • Triage is a numbered list of commands or console actions that take five minutes and end with a decision.
  • Diagnosis is a short decision tree, not an essay.
  • Mitigation lists actions, each with a command in backticks and a stop condition: how the responder knows the action worked, and when to stop doing it.
  • Escalation has a time trigger and a named rotation.
  • Verification states the number that should be true when the incident is over.
1fcfd02511:
Most inherited runbooks are missing the AI-specific content:

  • For a quality burn: which dashboard shows quality by segment, how to see which bundle is active and when it changed, how to roll back with one command, and how to sample twenty failures to look for a new input pattern.
  • For a cost spike: how to compare the rendered prompt between two bundle versions, and how to check the cache hit rate.
  • For a provider incident: how to switch the route to the fallback model, and what quality drop to expect from it.
  • For a refusal spike: how to tell a model change from a guardrail change from a prompt-injection campaign (ch 13).
  • For a deprecation notice: who opens the migration plan, and where the tracker is.

Each is an alert in the catalog, and each alert has exactly one runbook.
024bafe9f1:
Runbooks rot, so treat them as code. They live in the repository, in a format a linter can read. The linter runs in CI and also on a schedule, because staleness is a function of time rather than of commits.

These checks have caught real problems:

  • a missing section;
  • a missing front-matter field;
  • an owner that is a person's first name or the word 'someone';
  • no command in the mitigation;
  • no stop condition;
  • no time trigger in the escalation;
  • wording like 'ask the AI team' or 'look at the dashboard' that points at nothing;
  • a last-reviewed date older than 90 days;
  • an alert name that is not in the alert catalog;
  • and, in the other direction, alerts that have no runbook.
343fc7a305:
The two good runbooks pass. The three bad ones show the typical failure modes.

'Provider problems' has an owner of 'someone', no impact section, and a mitigation that says to ask the AI team. That is a runbook written for the one case where it cannot work: the AI team is on holiday, and the responder must decide alone.

'Refusal rate spike' mitigates by editing the prompt in production. That bypasses every control in sections 11 to 14. The linter catches it only as 'no stop condition' and 'no rollback'. If your team is prone to this, add a lint rule for that phrase.

The five alerts without a runbook are the more serious finding. An alert with no runbook is a page with no action.
76746afcfd:
On-call design is arithmetic about attention. The classic guidance from site reliability engineering has two parts. An engineer on a shift should handle a small number of actionable incidents; the SRE book suggests at most two per 12-hour shift. And most pages should lead to action.

The quantity that matters is page precision: the share of pages that were real. A page that is not real teaches the engineer to ignore the next one.

So the first on-call task is an estimate. For each alert, estimate the expected number of real pages and false pages a month. Fix any alert with precision under about 50 percent before it goes live.
70f95b47ba:
The estimate comes from the structure of each alert.

A burn-rate alert evaluated every five minutes performs about 8,640 tests a month. If each has a false-alarm probability of 0.002 percent, that is 0.17 false pages a month. A quality alert on a 6-hour window, evaluated 120 times a month with a false-alarm probability of 0.1 percent, adds 0.12.

Compare the naive alert 'daily pass rate below target'. It performs 30 tests with a false-alarm probability of 50 percent. That is 15 false pages a month for 0.5 real ones: a precision of 3 percent.

The refusal-rate alert in the example has a precision of 29 percent, because its threshold is a point estimate on small counts. It needs the same interval treatment as the quality alert.
d767541c71:
Once the alerts are clean, the expected load is about 3.6 real pages a month. That number decides the staffing question.

A dedicated 24x7 rotation of eight people for 3.6 pages a month is waste. Each engineer would be on call for 90 hours a month to receive one page every two months.

The efficient design is to attach the AI alerts to the existing platform rotation. Train that rotation with the runbooks, and rehearse the rollback. Then name a second-line AI-quality contact who is reachable within 30 minutes.

If the service is large enough to need its own rotation, size it from the per-person on-call cap your organisation sets. Consider follow-the-sun across two regions to remove night shifts. Remember that handoffs between regions need the same runbooks and the same registry (ch 10 covers the dashboards both regions need).
90a2fa531c:
The safety and compliance row is the one the exam rewards. Suppose the failing segment is the one with a regulatory or contractual floor (in the example, dispute handling). Then the segment sets the severity, not the size of the burn.

The mitigation order is also fixed. Restore the last known good state first: rollback, fail-over, or the kill switch from ch 13. Diagnose second. An incident commander who starts by reading logs while the bad bundle is still serving customers has the order backwards.
6dd117bea1:
Retirement is the lifecycle phase teams skip. It matters because of accumulation. A system that never retires bundles piles up risks:

  • deprecated versions that still hold credentials;
  • jobs that still reference models the provider has stopped serving;
  • dashboards for things that no longer exist;
  • logs that outlive their retention basis;
  • prompts that nobody can say are safe to delete.

Each of those is a risk with an owner nobody remembers. Retirement closes those loops deliberately, in an order, with a check that stops it going wrong.
f9630801d1:
There are three kinds of retirement to distinguish. Retiring a bundle (a superseded prompt-and-model combination) happens routinely, after the rollback window. Retiring a model pin across the estate happens when the provider retires the snapshot; it ends a vendor-upgrade programme. Retiring a service is the full shutdown: customer notice, data disposition, evidence of deletion.

The nine preconditions in the example cover all three:

  • Traffic is drained to zero. A retirement that leaves 2 percent of traffic on the old bundle is a degradation.
  • Nothing in code, configuration or infrastructure-as-code references the bundle. The pin linter runs to zero findings.
  • The prompt text and hash are archived, with the evaluation results and golden-set version. An auditor may ask what a customer was told eighteen months ago.
  • Logs are retained or purged by the policy of ch 14, not by accident.
  • The system card is marked retired and points at its successor.
  • Dashboards and alerts for the bundle are removed, so nobody investigates a silent panel.
  • The credentials and grants scoped to it are revoked.
  • And the owner acknowledges.
48e52eed8d:
Everything above ports directly. The arithmetic (burn rate, Wilson interval, paired test) is plain Java. The companion folder has compiled and tested ports of the burn-rate check and the registry state machine.

What a Spring service adds is the wiring:

  • meters that emit the SLIs;
  • configuration that carries the bundle;
  • a start-up guard that refuses to boot on an unpinned or tampered bundle;
  • rules in the metrics backend.

The code in this section sketches that wiring, against Spring Boot and Micrometer. It was not compiled in the companion, so check property names and dependency versions against your Boot version (check the docs).
d9d59f81f0:
Three Spring-specific notes.

Put the bundle id in the logging MDC at the start of each request, so every log line carries it (ch 10).

Implement the canary as a weighted router bean that reads the traffic share from the registry or a feature-flag service. Make the share and the bundle ids part of the span attributes, so quality and latency can be sliced by bundle.

And make rollback a configuration change that every pod picks up without a restart: Spring Cloud Config refresh, a flag service, or a registry poll. A rollback that needs a redeploy is the slow path you designed section 13 to avoid.
933d15c047:
None of the machinery in this chapter needs a model to test. That is the point of building it as arithmetic over counts and records. The tests worth writing are properties of the machinery:

  • The SLO library: burn rate of exactly the allowed fraction is 1; a window with no events has burn 0; the Wilson interval contains the point estimate and widens as n shrinks; min_detectable_burn decreases as n grows.
  • The registry: an alias is refused; a duplicate is refused; promotion skipping a state is refused; there is never more than one active bundle; rollback returns the previous bundle and fails if it is not servable; an in-place edit to prompt text is detected.
  • The gate: a candidate identical to the baseline is admitted; a candidate with a 5-point drop in a high-risk segment is rejected even if the aggregate improves; a segment below min_n yields HOLD; noise above the flake limit rejects.
  • The runbook linter: each broken fixture produces its expected findings, and the shipped good fixtures stay clean.
  • The canary: a true regression is rolled back in stage 1; a true no-change candidate reaches 100 percent.
d0b826a2df:
Run these as ordinary unit tests in CI. Property-style tests with simulated data catch calibration mistakes in the statistics, such as using a one-sided z where a two-sided one is needed. The companion examples work this way: they assert on their own outputs.

One place does involve a model: the replay of production prompts. There, use a fake client with scripted responses, as example 17 does. That tests the harness's own logic separately from any real model behaviour (ch 11 covers live evaluation).
3a3ee2a1e4: CCAR-P presents scenarios with four plausible options and asks for the best architectural judgement. In this domain the right answer usually replaces something weak with something firm: an opinion with a measurement, a guarantee with an objective, or an in-place edit with a gated change. Work each scenario before you read the reasoning.
c28b30bd17:
The clause promises a property the team cannot define: accuracy on which distribution, judged by whom? Nor can the team measure it without noise. A 400-sample day has a 95 percent interval of about plus or minus 2.3 points around 94 percent. And the model can change on the provider's schedule.

Committing to method, report and remediation puts the promise in what the team controls. A moves the risk to engineering and still leaves the metric undefined. C reduces noise but not ambiguity, and it costs ten times as much judging. D lowers the number but keeps every problem of definition and noise. See sections 05 and 10.
0c098e76d7:
Availability and latency are green because the failure is a well-formed wrong answer. Only a quality SLI sees that. The timing points at a change. The registry shows which bundle became active and when, and the rollback is a pointer flip.

A fixes a problem the data says does not exist. C does not guarantee determinism, and it does nothing about a wrong answer that is consistently wrong. D shifts the burden to the customer. See sections 03, 05 and 13.
c732f384d3:
The segment has a literal floor, and the candidate is below it with evidence: a lower bound of the difference of minus 4.8 points, against a 2-point margin.

A canary (C) cannot see a 2.5-point drop. At 400 samples the interval is about plus or minus 3 points, so the regression would reach customers undetected. The gate exists to catch what the canary cannot.

If the old model is still served, a per-segment route that keeps it for disputes is a sound interim design. It is worth offering as a follow-up. D hides the problem inside a weighted number. See sections 14 and 15.
f3d6eecec4:
The provider fixes the retirement date. A 61-day critical path against a 68-day calendar has 7 days of slack, well under the 25 percent rule. Waiting for the next quarter means an outage.

An alias cannot extend a retirement. Requesting an extension may be worth doing in parallel, but it is not a plan. See section 16, and check the provider's deprecation policy for what is and is not negotiable.
137cb25744:
The control must make the unreviewed state impossible, not merely documented. An immutable bundle plus start-up hash verification means the live prompt always has a hash, an owner, an evaluation and a log line.

A and D document a bypass. C reduces who can bypass, and it slows the 02:00 mitigation without making the record reliable. See sections 11 to 13 and 18.
eefe7df805:
With the system exactly at target, a point-estimate alert pages on about half the days. The monthly SLO is met, which tells you the pages were noise. Burn-rate windows with minimum samples and intervals page only when the budget is draining fast enough to matter. The slow burn becomes a ticket.

A hides real regressions. C reduces noise by a factor of about three, at ten times the cost, and it still pages on a point estimate. D removes the alert at the hours when response is slowest. See sections 05, 09 and 19.
11476835d5: Day 0: clock and owner. The platform lead is accountable for the migration (RACI row). The pin linter finds three bundles that reference the model, with path lengths of 22, 38 and 15 days. The backward plan has 61 days of critical path on a 68-day calendar. That leaves 7 days of slack, 10 percent. Under the 25 percent rule the verdict is START NOW, and the dispute assistant's latest start is day 23.
96a7e99405: Day 7: candidate and first gate run. Run the golden set (1,360 items, two runs each for flake) on the candidate with the unchanged prompt. The aggregate improves from 94.1 to 95.5 percent, with a cost ratio of 1.00 and flake of 0.8 percent. But the dispute segment is 2.5 points worse, with a lower bound of minus 4.8 against a 2-point margin. Verdict: REJECT.
961260e261: Day 8: the decision. There are three options, with numbers. (a) Ship to four segments and keep the old model for disputes. That works as an interim, but not past day 68, because the old model retires. (b) Adapt the prompt for the dispute segment on the new model, as a separate C1 change. (c) Choose a different candidate. The team does (b). It also starts the per-segment route from (a) as the interim, so the four improved segments can ship early.
faa25eef38: Days 8 to 26: golden-set top-up. 880 additional labelled dispute items (about $3,300) take the segment from 360 to 1,240. That is enough to certify a 2-point margin at a discordant rate of 8 percent. It is a one-time cost that every later upgrade reuses, and that is the line in the ADR.
cbb5c86234: Days 26 to 40: prompt adaptation. Three prompt revisions follow, each a C1 change gated alone. The third restores the dispute pass rate to 93.9 percent, with a difference of +1.1 and a lower bound of minus 1.2 on the larger set: ADMIT TO CANARY. The behaviour diff on replayed traffic finds the fenced-JSON problem (11.7 percent strict-parse failures). The parser is made tolerant as a separate change.
8a09b4d8cb: Days 54 to 61: canary and cutover. The stages are 1, 5, 25 and 100 percent, with 24-hour minimum holds, judged at 100, 50, 10 and 1 percent. The candidate advances at every stage. The budget is checked before each stage: 78 percent of the quality budget remains, above the 50 percent line, so the policy allows it.
f112e7ac1d: Day 68 and after: retirement. The old bundle's nine preconditions are checked. The archive, the successor link on the system card and the credential revocation are done. The system card for the new bundle records the per-segment table, the golden-set version and the change history.
c54e09ee59: The pattern in that last paragraph is the Domain 6 communication skill. It has a date, a headline number, the one risk named with its mitigation and its price, and the fallback decision with a trigger date. It is a decision memo, not a status report.
e4a9ef600b: Availability. Budget: 0.5 percent of 150,000 = 750 bad requests a month, or 3.6 hours of full outage. The pages use the standard 1 h / 5 min at 14.4 and 6 h / 30 min at 6. At 150,000 a month (about 3.5 requests a minute), a 5-minute window holds about 17 requests. So a burn of 14.4 needs only one failure in the window. Require at least 10 requests in each window, and accept that the long window carries the decision at night.
27c2e8bbbb: Latency. SLI: share of chat requests within 5 seconds, objective 95 percent. Histogram buckets sit at 2, 3, 5 and 8 seconds, per request class (plain answers, and answers that call the outage-status tool). Budget: 7,500 slow requests a month. The tool-calling class gets its own objective, because its mean is two to three times that of plain answers.
b5f7f3be7d: Quality. 200 samples a day, stratified so that restoration-estimate answers (about 20 percent of traffic) get 80 of them. Take the aggregate first, with an SLO of 95 percent. A 6-hour window has 50 samples and can only see a burn of about 4.6. So the fast quality page uses 12 h / 2 h at a burn of 5. The slow ticket uses 7 days (1,400 samples, detectable burn about 1.4) at a burn of 1.5. Now the estimate segment. Its 80 daily samples give a 3-day window of 240, and a detectable burn of about 2.2 against a 7 percent allowance. That is wide, so the segment floor is checked on a 7-day window, and the segment's alert is a ticket, not a page. Be honest with the product owner: a 2-point drop in the estimate segment will take about a week to prove. The compensating control is the release gate, which is where those drops are caught.
f21b523977: SLA. Commit externally to availability of 99.0 percent and to the latency percentile on the plain-answer class. Offer a monthly SLI report with per-segment quality. Add a remediation clause for the estimate segment: a plan within 5 business days if a 7-day window falls below 93 percent. No accuracy guarantee.
29c9643805: Documentation and ownership. The SLO spec lives in the repository, with the linter in CI. There are runbooks for the five alerts. The system card is generated at each release. The provider's deprecation feed is assigned to the platform lead. A rollback rehearsal runs on a 90-day calendar.
810aaa9c43: What the pack cannot see. Three things: slow quality drift under 1.4 burn; anything in a segment smaller than the sample can resolve; and wrong answers that the judge scores as correct (judge calibration against human labels is scheduled quarterly, ch 11). Write these three limits in the system card.
